sentences.text: Nanotyrannus possessed a slender, low skull with small crests or horns in front of the eyes, contrasting with the robust skull of Tyrannosaurus.
Its total length has been estimated at about 6 m, while a later estimate gave a length of roughly 5.5 m and a height of 2 m.
The postorbital bone lacks a cornual process, an unusual feature among advanced tyrannosaurs.
The fourth trochanter of the femur is parallel to the shaft rather than forming a peak.
The upper jaw held 14–15 teeth per side and the lower jaw 16 per side.
If fully grown, Nanotyrannus may have weighed around 1,200 kg, with the maximum possible body mass estimated at roughly 1,500 kg.
Its hind limbs were hyper-cursorial, suggesting a lifestyle adapted to pursuit predation.
The specimen nicknamed "Bloody Mary" has arm bones almost three feet long, and its hand bones are one and a half times longer than those of the famous Tyrannosaurus rex specimen "Sue".
Gilmoretyrannus is a newly named genus and combination of a tyrannosauroid dinosaur described by Sancarlo and Paul.
Nanotyrannus fossils are primarily known from the Hell Creek Formation.
The holotype skull (CMNH 7541) was collected in 1942 by David Hosbrook Dunkle and described by Gilmore in 1946 as Gorgosaurus lancensis.
The juvenile tyrannosaur specimen "Jane" (BMRP 2002.4.1) was discovered in 2001 and was initially thought to belong to Nanotyrannus.
Large muscle-attachment sites at the back of the skull suggest it could flex its head strongly side-to-side.
Rear skull muscle attachment sites were especially large, indicating a capacity for great lateral head movement.
Longer legs and relatively larger forelimbs indicate Nanotyrannus was likely a pursuit predator.
Its forelimbs were proportionally longer than those of contemporary tyrannosaurs, supporting a more active predatory role.
Front upper-jaw teeth lacked serrations, a condition called ziphodonty not seen in other tyrannosaurids, implying a different feeding strategy.
CT scans of "Jane"'s braincase reveal differences in blood-vessel and optic-nerve canal positions compared with Tyrannosaurus rex, which may reflect distinct sensory capabilities.
The left side of the reconstructed skull of "Jane" shows puncture marks on the upper jaw that have been interpreted as bite wounds from a conspecific.
CT scans confirmed that these puncture wounds were traumatic injuries that later healed.
Facial lesions on "Jane" differ structurally from parasite-induced lesions found on the adult Tyrannosaurus specimen "Sue", which occur on the lower jaw.
The genus Nanotyrannus was formally named by Bakker, Williams and Currie in 1988.
Nanotyrannus is the sole definitive member of the family Nanotyrannidae, though some analyses link it with Appalachiosaurus and Dryptosaurus.
Maximum-parsimony analysis placed Moros intrepidus as the sister taxon to the Nanotyrannus holotype "Jane".
The type locality of Gilmoretyrannus is the Lance and Hell Creek formations in Montana and Wyoming, United States.
Nanotyrannus lived in western North America about 67 million years ago during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous.
The most recent common ancestor of Nanotyrannidae and Tyrannosauridae may have lived about 103 million years ago, around the formation of the Western Interior Seaway.
Many researchers consider the Nanotyrannus skull to belong to an immature Tyrannosaurus rex, making its taxonomic status controversial.
The first suggestion that the Nanotyrannus holotype might be a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex was made by Rozhdestvensky in 1965.
Researchers argue that the number of teeth may vary individually and is not a reliable indicator of growth stage.
Paleontologists Currie and Williams, who had previously supported Nanotyrannus lancensis as a valid species, later interpreted "Jane" as confirming that Nanotyrannus was actually a juvenile T. rex.
A 2016 limb-proportion analysis suggested Nanotyrannus specimens show varying degrees of cursoriality, which was proposed as a possible taxonomic difference from T. rex.
